papers.research_question: Can we systematically amplify safety alignment in LLMs by permanently steering activations toward the refusal-mediating subspace?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces RANK-ONE SAFETY INJECTION (ROSI), a fine-tuning-free weight-editing method that amplifies safety alignment in LLMs by permanently steering activations toward a refusal-mediating subspace.
papers.conclusion: ROSI is a simple, effective, and interpretable method to enhance LLM safety, demonstrating the practical value of mechanistic interpretability for designing efficient safety interventions.
papers.key_findings:
ROSI consistently improves harm refusal rates in aligned models while preserving utility on standard benchmarks.
ROSI makes aligned models more robust to a suite of adversarial jailbreak attacks.
ROSI can inject safety into uncensored models (e.g., DOLPHIN), effectively re-aligning them without retraining.
The safety direction is largely orthogonal to utility representations, allowing safety amplification with minimal side effects.
A safety system prompt is crucial for extracting a meaningful safety direction from uncensored models.
papers.limitation: Smaller models (≤ 1B) show the biggest degradation in benign compliance (BC) when applying ROSI.
future_direction: Exploring more sophisticated methods for identifying and manipulating conceptual directions
Extending the approach to other desirable model attributes beyond safety, such as honesty or controllability
papers.abstract: Safety alignment in Large Language Models (LLMs) often involves mediating internal representations to refuse harmful requests. Recent research has demonstrated that these safety mechanisms can be bypassed by ablating or removing specific representational directions within the model. In this paper, we propose the opposite approach: Rank-One Safety Injection (ROSI), a white-box method that amplifies a model's safety alignment by permanently steering its activations toward the refusal-mediating subspace. ROSI operates as a simple, fine-tuning-free rank-one weight modification applied to all residual stream write matrices. The required safety direction can be computed from a small set of harmful and harmless instruction pairs. We show that ROSI consistently increases safety refusal rates - as evaluated by Llama Guard 3 - while preserving the utility of the model on standard benchmarks such as MMLU, HellaSwag, and Arc. Furthermore, we show that ROSI can also re-align 'uncensored' models by amplifying their own latent safety directions, demonstrating its utility as an effective last-mile safety procedure. Our results suggest that targeted, interpretable weight steering is a cheap and potent mechanism to improve LLM safety, complementing more resource-intensive fine-tuning paradigms.

papers.title: From Directions to Cones: Exploring Multidimensional Representations of Propositional Facts in LLMs
papers.research_question: Does truth in LLMs have a multi-dimensional representation (concept cone) rather than a single linear direction, and can such cones causally mediate truth-related behavior?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that truth in LLMs is represented as a multi-dimensional cone in activation space, and that interventions using these cones can reliably steer model outputs on true/false propositions while preserving unrelated capabilities.
papers.conclusion: Multi-dimensional concept cones can reliably steer LLM behavior on true/false propositions across architectures and sizes, revealing a robust subspace of activation vectors that modulate factuality.
papers.key_findings:
Truth-related directions are localized in middle to later layers, with the final token position being most effective for interventions.
Multi-dimensional concept cones for truth exist and can causally mediate truthful behavior across different model families and sizes.
Increasing cone dimensionality generally improves steering effectiveness, but beyond a point, ASR declines, especially in smaller models.
The discovered truth directions are specific and do not significantly affect general instruction-following capabilities (low KL divergence on Alpaca).
The classic DIM direction aligns only with the first axis of the cone; other axes are orthogonal, indicating additional structure.
papers.limitation:
Experiments were conducted on relatively small open-source models (1.5B–7B parameters) and may not generalize to larger frontier models.
The operationalization of truth is narrow, limited to simple unambiguous propositional facts, and does not capture more complex notions of truth.
The method does not guarantee discovery of a maximally informative or interpretable subspace, and individual cone axes lack semantic meaning.
future_direction: Pair cones with automated clustering or sparse autoencoding to assign semantic meaning to basis vectors.
Extend the method to larger, instruction-tuned models.
Extend to multimodal settings.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) exhibit strong conversational abilities but often generate falsehoods. Prior work suggests that the truthfulness of simple propositions can be represented as a single linear direction in a model's internal activations, but this may not fully capture its underlying geometry. In this work, we extend the concept cone framework, recently introduced for modeling refusal, to the domain of truth. We identify multi-dimensional cones that causally mediate truth-related behavior across multiple LLM families. Our results are supported by three lines of evidence: (i) causal interventions reliably flip model responses to factual statements, (ii) learned cones generalize across model architectures, and (iii) cone-based interventions preserve unrelated model behavior. These findings reveal the richer, multidirectional structure governing simple true/false propositions in LLMs and highlight concept cones as a promising tool for probing abstract behaviors.

papers.title: No Two Devils Alike: Unveiling Distinct Mechanisms of Fine-tuning Attacks
papers.research_question: While different fine-tuning attacks can all significantly compromise safety, do their attack mechanisms exhibit strong similarities?
papers.core_contribution: The paper reveals that two representative fine-tuning attacks (Explicit Harmful Attack and Identity-Shifting Attack) have distinct mechanisms for compromising an LLM's safety alignment, indicating the need for diverse defense strategies.
papers.conclusion: Different fine-tuning attacks exploit distinct mechanisms to compromise LLM safety, underscoring the need for varied and robust defense strategies.
papers.key_findings:
EHA aggressively disrupts the harmful instruction recognition stage by suppressing the transmission of harmful signals in upper layers, while ISA does not significantly impact this stage.
Both EHA and ISA disrupt the initial refusal tone generation, but EHA suppresses refusal tokens via MLPs in mid-layers, whereas ISA does not.
Both attacks impair the refusal response completion stage, with ISA having a greater impact, causing the model to persistently generate harmful content even with refusal prefixes.
Adding a safety-oriented system prompt only partially mitigates the impairment caused by the attacks.
The attacks cause representation shifts: EHA shifts representations more for harmful inputs, while ISA causes a shift orthogonal to the harmfulness direction.
papers.limitation:
The study only investigates two fine-tuning attacks (EHA and ISA), which do not encompass the full spectrum of possible attacks.
The analysis is conducted solely on Llama-2-7b-chat, limiting the generalizability of the findings to other models.
The investigation does not involve the mechanics of particular components (e.g., individual attention heads) due to scope constraints.
future_direction: Using trained probes at mid-layers to robustly detect harmful inputs without an external detector.
Developing more attack-resisting model manipulation methods for safeguarding, as current steering methods may be less effective on attacked models.
papers.abstract: The existing safety alignment of Large Language Models (LLMs) is found fragile and could be easily attacked through different strategies, such as through fine-tuning on a few harmful examples or manipulating the prefix of the generation results. However, the attack mechanisms of these strategies are still underexplored. In this paper, we ask the following question: \textit{while these approaches can all significantly compromise safety, do their attack mechanisms exhibit strong similarities?} To answer this question, we break down the safeguarding process of an LLM when encountered with harmful instructions into three stages: (1) recognizing harmful instructions, (2) generating an initial refusing tone, and (3) completing the refusal response. Accordingly, we investigate whether and how different attack strategies could influence each stage of this safeguarding process. We utilize techniques such as logit lens and activation patching to identify model components that drive specific behavior, and we apply cross-model probing to examine representation shifts after an attack. In particular, we analyze the two most representative types of attack approaches: Explicit Harmful Attack (EHA) and Identity-Shifting Attack (ISA). Surprisingly, we find that their attack mechanisms diverge dramatically. Unlike ISA, EHA tends to aggressively target the harmful recognition stage. While both EHA and ISA disrupt the latter two stages, the extent and mechanisms of their attacks differ significantly. Our findings underscore the importance of understanding LLMs' internal safeguarding process and suggest that diverse defense mechanisms are required to effectively cope with various types of attacks.

papers.title: Mitigating Object Hallucinations in Large Vision-Language Models via Attention Calibration
papers.research_question: How can object hallucination in Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) be mitigated by addressing spatial perception bias in attention maps?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Dynamic Attention Calibration (DAC), a lightweight, plug-and-play module that dynamically calibrates vision token attention to mitigate spatial perception bias and reduce object hallucination in LVLMs.
papers.conclusion: Attention calibration, specifically through the proposed Dynamic Attention Calibration (DAC) module, is a promising strategy for mitigating object hallucination in LVLMs by dynamically addressing spatial perception bias.
papers.key_findings:
DAC significantly reduces object hallucination on POPE benchmarks, achieving state-of-the-art performance across Random, Popular, and Adversarial settings.
DAC improves performance on the CHAIR metric for open-ended image captioning, reducing hallucinated objects in generated descriptions.
DAC enhances general perception capabilities on the MME benchmark, particularly in object-level and attribute-level tasks.
DAC maintains or improves performance on the LLaVA-Bench, indicating it does not degrade general vision-language understanding.
The method is effective across multiple LVLM architectures (LLaVA-1.5, mPLUG-Owl2, LLaVA-NeXT), demonstrating generalizability.
papers.limitation: DAC's performance may be limited when validation data is scarce.
future_direction: Explore data-free calibration methods.
Extend attention calibration to further improve LVLMs reliability.
papers.abstract: Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) exhibit impressive multimodal reasoning capabilities but remain highly susceptible to object hallucination, where models generate responses that are not factually aligned with the visual content. Recent works attribute this issue to an inherent bias of LVLMs where vision token attention map has a fixed correlation with spatial position, and propose to mitigate this issue by reordering visual tokens. However, we find that different LVLMs exhibit different correlations between attention and spatial position, which makes the existing solution difficult to generalize to other LVLMs. To address this issue, we first introduce a training-free solution, Uniform Attention Calibration (UAC), that estimates the bias from single meaningless input image and applies a calibration matrix to rectify attention imbalances. To further alleviate the bias, we relax the assumption of single meaningless input in UAC and introduce a fine-tuning solution, Dynamic Attention Calibration (DAC), that enforces the consistent outputs wherever the object locates in the image via a plug-and-plays module. Comprehensive experiments across multiple benchmarks demonstrate that UAC and DAC significantly reduce object hallucination while improving general multimodal alignment. Our methods achieve state-of-the-art performance across diverse LVLM architectures on various metrics.

papers.title: CoT is Not the Chain of Truth: An Empirical Internal Analysis of Reasoning LLMs for Fake News Generation
papers.research_question: Does Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning in LLMs contain unsafe internal reasoning patterns even when the model's final output refuses a harmful request?
papers.core_contribution: The paper reveals that CoT reasoning in LLMs often contains unsafe internal narratives even when the model refuses harmful requests, and introduces a framework to localize safety-critical layers and attention heads using Jacobian-based spectral metrics.
papers.conclusion: CoT is not inherently safe, and surface-level refusal does not guarantee safety in the internal reasoning process; the proposed framework provides a mechanistic understanding to mitigate latent reasoning risks.
papers.key_findings:
Approximately 80% of reasoning chains harbor latent security risks even when models refuse harmful requests.
Safety-critical routing decisions are concentrated in a few contiguous mid-depth layers.
Jacobian-based metrics (stability, geometry, energy) can identify critical attention heads responsible for unsafe reasoning.
Perturbing critical attention heads leads to safety degradation, confirming their causal role in unsafe reasoning.
papers.abstract: From generating headlines to fabricating news, the Large Language Models (LLMs) are typically assessed by their final outputs, under the safety assumption that a refusal response signifies safe reasoning throughout the entire process. Challenging this assumption, our study reveals that during fake news generation, even when a model rejects a harmful request, its Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning may still internally contain and propagate unsafe narratives. To analyze this phenomenon, we introduce a unified safety-analysis framework that systematically deconstructs CoT generation across model layers and evaluates the role of individual attention heads through Jacobian-based spectral metrics. Within this framework, we introduce three interpretable measures: stability, geometry, and energy to quantify how specific attention heads respond or embed deceptive reasoning patterns. Extensive experiments on multiple reasoning-oriented LLMs show that the generation risk rise significantly when the thinking mode is activated, where the critical routing decisions concentrated in only a few contiguous mid-depth layers. By precisely identifying the attention heads responsible for this divergence, our work challenges the assumption that refusal implies safety and provides a new understanding perspective for mitigating latent reasoning risks.

papers.title: Inference-Time Intervention: Eliciting Truthful Answers from a Language Model
papers.research_question: How can we enhance the truthfulness of large language models by intervening on their activations during inference?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Inference-Time Intervention (ITI), a minimally invasive technique that shifts activations along truthful directions in attention heads during inference to improve model truthfulness.
papers.conclusion: ITI is a promising, efficient method for improving truthfulness in LLMs, suggesting that models internally represent truth which can be elicited through activation shifts.
papers.key_findings:
ITI significantly improves truthfulness on the TruthfulQA benchmark, e.g., increasing Alpaca's truthfulness from 32.5% to 65.1%.
There is a trade-off between truthfulness and helpfulness that can be balanced by tuning intervention strength.
ITI is data-efficient, requiring only a few hundred examples to find truthful directions.
ITI generalizes to other question-answering benchmarks (Natural Questions, TriviaQA, MMLU) with smaller improvements.
LLMs appear to have an internal representation of truth even when generating falsehoods.
papers.limitation:
ITI is not sufficient for ensuring truthful answers from LLMs and should be part of a more comprehensive approach.
There is a trade-off between truthfulness and helpfulness; increasing truthfulness may reduce informativeness.
future_direction: Test ITI on a wider variety of benchmarks beyond TruthfulQA.
Investigate the mechanistic understanding of what ITI does to internal representations.
papers.abstract: We introduce Inference-Time Intervention (ITI), a technique designed to enhance the "truthfulness" of large language models (LLMs). ITI operates by shifting model activations during inference, following a set of directions across a limited number of attention heads. This intervention significantly improves the performance of LLaMA models on the TruthfulQA benchmark. On an instruction-finetuned LLaMA called Alpaca, ITI improves its truthfulness from 32.5% to 65.1%. We identify a tradeoff between truthfulness and helpfulness and demonstrate how to balance it by tuning the intervention strength. ITI is minimally invasive and computationally inexpensive. Moreover, the technique is data efficient: while approaches like RLHF require extensive annotations, ITI locates truthful directions using only few hundred examples. Our findings suggest that LLMs may have an internal representation of the likelihood of something being true, even as they produce falsehoods on the surface.

papers.title: The Internal State of an LLM Knows When It's Lying
papers.research_question: Can the internal state of an LLM be used to reveal the truthfulness of statements, both provided to and generated by the LLM?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that LLM internal activations contain information about statement truthfulness and introduces SAPLMA, a classifier that uses these activations to detect false statements with higher accuracy than baselines like few-shot prompting.
papers.conclusion: SAPLMA leverages LLM hidden activations to predict statement truthfulness, offering a way to filter false information and increase trust in LLM-generated content.
papers.key_findings:
SAPLMA achieves accuracy between 60% to 80% on specific topics with OPT-6.7b and 70% to 90% with LLAMA2-7b, outperforming few-shot prompting which maxes at 56% accuracy.
The optimal hidden layer for SAPLMA varies between models, e.g., 20th layer for OPT-6.7b and middle layer for LLAMA2-7b.
Sentence probability assigned by the LLM is not a reliable indicator of truthfulness due to dependencies on sentence length and word frequencies.
SAPLMA can classify both externally provided statements and those generated by the LLM itself.
The method does not require fine-tuning the LLM, using only a trained classifier on frozen activations.
papers.limitation:
The method detects binary true/false, but in practice, detecting uncertainty or confidence levels might be more useful.
Tested only in English; applicability to multilingual settings is not verified.
For longer responses, activation values might need decoupling to isolate the most recent statement.
future_direction: Apply SAPLMA to larger LLMs and conduct human interaction experiments.
Study how activations develop over time as additional words are generated.
Extend to multilingual input and test cross-language applicability.
papers.abstract: While Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown exceptional performance in various tasks, one of their most prominent drawbacks is generating inaccurate or false information with a confident tone. In this paper, we provide evidence that the LLM's internal state can be used to reveal the truthfulness of statements. This includes both statements provided to the LLM, and statements that the LLM itself generates. Our approach is to train a classifier that outputs the probability that a statement is truthful, based on the hidden layer activations of the LLM as it reads or generates the statement. Experiments demonstrate that given a set of test sentences, of which half are true and half false, our trained classifier achieves an average of 71\% to 83\% accuracy labeling which sentences are true versus false, depending on the LLM base model. Furthermore, we explore the relationship between our classifier's performance and approaches based on the probability assigned to the sentence by the LLM. We show that while LLM-assigned sentence probability is related to sentence truthfulness, this probability is also dependent on sentence length and the frequencies of words in the sentence, resulting in our trained classifier providing a more reliable approach to detecting truthfulness, highlighting its potential to enhance the reliability of LLM-generated content and its practical applicability in real-world scenarios.

papers.title: Representational Stability of Truth in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How stable are LLM truth judgments under controlled semantic perturbations, and does internal representational stability predict behavioral stability? The paper investigates the role of epistemic familiarity in belief stability.
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the P-StaT framework to evaluate belief stability in LLMs under semantic perturbations, and shows that epistemic familiarity (familiar vs. unfamiliar fictional content) governs stability in both representational and behavioral settings.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that epistemic familiarity is a robust signal for belief stability in LLMs, and that the P-StaT framework complements accuracy-based factuality evaluation with a notion of epistemic robustness.
papers.key_findings:
Unfamiliar Synthetic content induces the largest epistemic retractions in both representational and behavioral evaluations.
Familiar Fictional content is more representationally distinct and produces fewer retractions.
There is a decoupling between linguistic similarity and latent-space organization for Fictional content.
The stability hierarchy (Synthetic most destabilizing) is consistent across domains and LLMs.
Representational stability under probing perturbations predicts behavioral stability under zero-shot perturbations.
papers.limitation: Zero-shot retractions conflate belief changes with the number of baseline beliefs available to retract, making direct comparison with probing results difficult.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are widely used for factual tasks such as "What treats asthma?" or "What is the capital of Latvia?". However, it remains unclear how stably LLMs encode distinctions between true, false, and neither-true-nor-false content in their internal probabilistic representations. We introduce representational stability as the robustness of an LLM's veracity representations to perturbations in the operational definition of truth. We assess representational stability by (i) training a linear probe on an LLM's activations to separate true from not-true statements and (ii) measuring how its learned decision boundary shifts under controlled label changes. Using activations from sixteen open-source models and three factual domains, we compare two types of neither statements. The first are fact-like assertions about entities we believe to be absent from any training data. We call these unfamiliar neither statements. The second are nonfactual claims drawn from well-known fictional contexts. We call these familiar neither statements. The unfamiliar statements induce the largest boundary shifts, producing up to $40\%$ flipped truth judgements in fragile domains (such as word definitions), while familiar fictional statements remain more coherently clustered and yield smaller changes ($\leq 8.2\%$). These results suggest that representational stability stems more from epistemic familiarity than from linguistic form. More broadly, our approach provides a diagnostic for auditing and training LLMs to preserve coherent truth assignments under semantic uncertainty, rather than optimizing for output accuracy alone.

papers.title: Unsupervised Real-Time Hallucination Detection based on the Internal States of Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Can hallucinations in large language models be detected in real-time using the models' internal states, without requiring manual annotations?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces MIND, an unsupervised framework for real-time hallucination detection using the internal states of LLMs, and HELM, a new benchmark for evaluating hallucination detection across multiple LLMs.
papers.conclusion: MIND is an effective unsupervised method for real-time hallucination detection, and the HELM benchmark facilitates future research in this area.
papers.key_findings:
MIND outperforms existing hallucination detection methods in terms of AUC and correlation.
MIND is highly efficient, taking only about 3% of the LLM's response generation time for detection.
Customized training data generated by the same LLM significantly improves hallucination detection performance.
The method is broadly effective across a variety of LLMs.
Using the contextualized embedding of the last token of the last layer is effective for hallucination detection.
papers.limitation: Detecting hallucinations using only the internal states of LLMs may not be as accurate as combining internal states with generated text.
future_direction: Integrating internal states of LLMs with generated text for improved hallucination detection.
papers.abstract: Hallucinations in large language models (LLMs) refer to the phenomenon of LLMs producing responses that are coherent yet factually inaccurate. This issue undermines the effectiveness of LLMs in practical applications, necessitating research into detecting and mitigating hallucinations of LLMs. Previous studies have mainly concentrated on post-processing techniques for hallucination detection, which tend to be computationally intensive and limited in effectiveness due to their separation from the LLM's inference process. To overcome these limitations, we introduce MIND, an unsupervised training framework that leverages the internal states of LLMs for real-time hallucination detection without requiring manual annotations. Additionally, we present HELM, a new benchmark for evaluating hallucination detection across multiple LLMs, featuring diverse LLM outputs and the internal states of LLMs during their inference process. Our experiments demonstrate that MIND outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods in hallucination detection.

papers.title: Beacon: Single-Turn Diagnosis and Mitigation of Latent Sycophancy in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How to diagnose and mitigate latent sycophancy in large language models using a forced-choice benchmark and activation steering?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the Beacon benchmark for diagnosing sycophancy in LLMs and demonstrates the use of activation steering for mitigation.
papers.conclusion: Beacon reframes sycophancy as a measurable form of normative misgeneralization, providing a reproducible foundation for studying and mitigating alignment drift in large-scale generative systems.
papers.key_findings:
Sycophancy decomposes into stable linguistic and affective sub-biases, each scaling with model capacity.
Prompt-level interventions reduce overt sycophantic behavior but have limited impact and can lead to residual errors or shifted failure modes.
Activation steering, particularly cluster-specific steering, can effectively modulate latent sycophantic biases by perturbing hidden states.
The Beacon benchmark provides a reproducible foundation for measuring alignment drift and studying sycophancy.
Sycophancy is encoded in identifiable representational structures amenable to mechanism-level mitigation.
future_direction: Exploration of internal policy geometries
Evaluation of layered mitigation strategies
Consistent benchmarking of novel generative systems
papers.abstract: Large language models internalize a structural trade-off between truthfulness and obsequious flattery, emerging from reward optimization that conflates helpfulness with polite submission. This latent bias, known as sycophancy, manifests as a preference for user agreement over principled reasoning. We introduce Beacon, a single-turn forced-choice benchmark that isolates this bias independent of conversational context, enabling precise measurement of the tension between factual accuracy and submissive bias. Evaluations across twelve state-of-the-art models reveal that sycophancy decomposes into stable linguistic and affective sub-biases, each scaling with model capacity. We further propose prompt-level and activation-level interventions that modulate these biases in opposing directions, exposing the internal geometry of alignment as a dynamic manifold between truthfulness and socially compliant judgment. Beacon reframes sycophancy as a measurable form of normative misgeneralization, providing a reproducible foundation for studying and mitigating alignment drift in large-scale generative systems.

papers.title: LLM Internal States Reveal Hallucination Risk Faced With a Query
papers.research_question: Whether LLMs can estimate their own hallucination risk before response generation using internal states.
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that LLM internal states can indicate whether a query was seen in training data and predict hallucination risk, achieving high accuracy with a probing estimator.
papers.conclusion: This work demonstrates that LLMs have latent self-assessment capabilities to estimate hallucination risks prior to response generation.
papers.key_findings:
Internal states can distinguish seen/unseen queries with 80.28% accuracy.
Internal states can estimate hallucination risk with 84.32% accuracy across 15 NLG tasks.
Layer depth positively correlates with prediction performance.
Internal states are model-specific but allow some zero-shot transfer.
Features in internal states are shared within tasks but not across tasks.
papers.limitation:
Lack of human evaluation in data labeling process.
Trade-off in performance compared to methods using both query and response.
papers.abstract: The hallucination problem of Large Language Models (LLMs) significantly limits their reliability and trustworthiness. Humans have a self-awareness process that allows us to recognize what we don't know when faced with queries. Inspired by this, our paper investigates whether LLMs can estimate their own hallucination risk before response generation. We analyze the internal mechanisms of LLMs broadly both in terms of training data sources and across 15 diverse Natural Language Generation (NLG) tasks, spanning over 700 datasets. Our empirical analysis reveals two key insights: (1) LLM internal states indicate whether they have seen the query in training data or not; and (2) LLM internal states show they are likely to hallucinate or not regarding the query. Our study explores particular neurons, activation layers, and tokens that play a crucial role in the LLM perception of uncertainty and hallucination risk. By a probing estimator, we leverage LLM self-assessment, achieving an average hallucination estimation accuracy of 84.32\% at run time.

papers.title: Who is In Charge? Dissecting Role Conflicts in Instruction Following
papers.research_question: How are role conflicts (system-user vs. social hierarchy) represented and resolved in large language models, and can steering vectors shift obedience?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that system-user conflicts are represented in a distinct subspace from social conflicts, with strong conflict detection but weak resolution for system-user, and that steering vectors amplify instruction following in a role-agnostic way.
papers.conclusion: System instructions are weakly enforced compared to social cues, highlighting the need for lightweight hierarchy-sensitive alignment methods to improve robustness.
papers.key_findings:
Linear probing shows conflict-decision signals are encoded early (around layer 10-12), with system-user and social conflicts forming distinct subspaces.
Logit attribution reveals that system-user conflicts have higher conflict detection (25.61% of cases show opposing signed contributions) but lower primary win rate given conflict (10.92%), while social consensus conflicts have lower conflict detection (16.42%) but higher primary win rate (71.74%).
Steering vectors derived from mean activations of social consensus vs. system-user conflicts amplify instruction following but in a role-agnostic way, not specifically restoring system obedience.
The model's obedience to system instructions is fragile compared to social cues, posing a safety risk for prompt-injection attacks.
The representation of conflict decisions is strongest in early layers and degrades in later layers as other generation-related computations are integrated.
papers.limitation: Steering vectors amplify instruction following in a role-agnostic way, not specifically restoring system obedience.
future_direction: Adapt prior work on attention boosting to selectively boost attention on system instructions while suppressing user instructions.
Use training-based methods to yield cleaner hierarchy-sensitive vectors.
Learn mappings between contrastive subspaces (e.g., system-user and CEO-intern) while preserving conflict detection.
papers.abstract: Large language models should follow hierarchical instructions where system prompts override user inputs, yet recent work shows they often ignore this rule while strongly obeying social cues such as authority or consensus. We extend these behavioral findings with mechanistic interpretations on a large-scale dataset. Linear probing shows conflict-decision signals are encoded early, with system-user and social conflicts forming distinct subspaces. Direct Logit Attribution reveals stronger internal conflict detection in system-user cases but consistent resolution only for social cues. Steering experiments show that, despite using social cues, the vectors surprisingly amplify instruction following in a role-agnostic way. Together, these results explain fragile system obedience and underscore the need for lightweight hierarchy-sensitive alignment methods.

papers.title: Adaptive Activation Steering: A Tuning-Free LLM Truthfulness Improvement Method for Diverse Hallucinations Categories
papers.research_question: This paper investigates how to improve the truthfulness of large language models by adaptively steering activations during inference, addressing the gap between what the model knows and what it tells, and handling diverse hallucination categories.
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Adaptive Activation Steering (ACT), a tuning-free method that improves LLM truthfulness by adaptively shifting activations toward truthful directions using diverse steering vectors and adaptive intensity control.
papers.conclusion: ACT is a tuning-free method that enhances LLM truthfulness by steering activations with diverse vectors and adaptive intensity, effectively addressing the gap between knowing and telling, and marks a promising advancement in reliable AI-generated content.
papers.key_findings:
ACT significantly improves truthfulness on TruthfulQA across multiple models (e.g., LLaMA, LLaMA2, Alpaca, Vicuna, LLaMA2-Chat, LLaMA3).
ACT's adaptive intensity control and diverse steering vectors are effective, outperforming existing baselines like ITI, CCS, RepE, and Mean-Centring.
ACT is orthogonal to few-shot prompting and instruction fine-tuning, and can be combined with them for further improvement.
ACT shows scalability across model sizes (7B to 65B), with consistent improvements.
ACT requires only a few dozen training samples and adds constant-time complexity during inference.
papers.limitation:
Applicability in real-world chat settings involving multi-turn conversations has not been fully explored.
The trade-off between truthfulness and helpfulness (e.g., the smoothness of generated text) is not explored.
future_direction: Explore ACT in multi-turn conversation settings.
Investigate the trade-off between truthfulness and helpfulness.
papers.abstract: Recent studies have indicated that Large Language Models (LLMs) harbor an inherent understanding of truthfulness, yet often fail to consistently express it and generate false statements. This gap between "knowing" and "telling" poses a challenge for ensuring the truthfulness of generated content. Inspired by recent work on the practice of encoding human-interpretable concepts linearly within large language models, we treat truthfulness as a specially linearly encoded concept within LLMs, and introduce Adaptive Activation Steering (ACT), a tuning-free method that adaptively shifts LLM's activations in the "truthful" direction during inference. ACT addresses diverse categories of hallucinations by utilizing diverse truthfulness-related steering vectors and adjusting the steering intensity adaptively. Applied as an add-on across various models, ACT significantly improves truthfulness in LLaMA ($\uparrow$ 142%), LLaMA2 ($\uparrow$ 24%), Alpaca ($\uparrow$ 36%), Vicuna ($\uparrow$ 28%), LLaMA2-Chat ($\uparrow$ 19%), and LLaMA3($\uparrow$ 34%). Furthermore, we verify ACT's scalability across larger models (13B, 33B, 65B), underscoring the adaptability of ACT to large-scale language models. Our code is available at https://github.com/tianlwang/ACT.

papers.title: Too Big to Fool: Resisting Deception in Language Models
papers.research_question: How do language models of varying capacities within the same family balance in-context information against their internal world models, particularly when faced with intentionally misleading prompts?
papers.core_contribution: Larger language models exhibit greater resilience to deceptive prompts, demonstrating an advanced ability to integrate conflicting in-context information with their internal knowledge, without simply ignoring prompts or relying on memorization.
papers.conclusion: The paper introduces an evaluation strategy that re-uses existing benchmarks with minimal changes to study LLM behavior. Experiments show that larger models are more resilient to deceptive prompts, indicating a better ability to integrate prompt information with internal knowledge.
papers.key_findings:
Larger models consistently show a smaller Relative Accuracy Drop when given deceptive hints, indicating higher resilience to misinformation.
Larger models do not ignore in-context information; they effectively follow legitimate instructions and utilize truthful hints.
The resilience is not due to memorization, as shown by control experiments with overfitted models and a model without prior exposure to the test data.
Larger models generally exhibit better instruction-following capabilities, except for the Gemma family which is an outlier.
Models can infer missing information from answer choices, maintaining accuracy above chance even when the question is removed.
papers.limitation:
The study focused exclusively on multiple-choice datasets, which may not capture nuances of open-ended or generative tasks.
Experiments involved only open-source LLMs, limiting generalizability to proprietary models with different architectures or training.
papers.abstract: Large language models must balance their weight-encoded knowledge with in-context information from prompts to generate accurate responses. This paper investigates this interplay by analyzing how models of varying capacities within the same family handle intentionally misleading in-context information. Our experiments demonstrate that larger models exhibit higher resilience to deceptive prompts, showcasing an advanced ability to interpret and integrate prompt information with their internal knowledge. Furthermore, we find that larger models outperform smaller ones in following legitimate instructions, indicating that their resilience is not due to disregarding in-context information. We also show that this phenomenon is likely not a result of memorization but stems from the models' ability to better leverage implicit task-relevant information from the prompt alongside their internally stored knowledge.

papers.title: Calibrating Verbal Uncertainty as a Linear Feature to Reduce Hallucinations
papers.research_question: How is verbal uncertainty represented in LLMs, and can calibrating it with semantic uncertainty detect and mitigate hallucinations?
papers.core_contribution: The paper discovers that verbal uncertainty in LLMs is mediated by a linear feature (VUF) and introduces Mechanistic Uncertainty Calibration (MUC) to calibrate verbal uncertainty with semantic uncertainty, reducing confident hallucinations by ~30%.
papers.conclusion: The work demonstrates that verbal uncertainty is a linear feature in LLMs, and calibrating it with semantic uncertainty through MUC effectively reduces confident hallucinations, making LLMs more trustworthy.
papers.key_findings:
Verbal uncertainty in LLMs is governed by a single linear direction (VUF) in the representation space, extractable via difference-in-means.
The mismatch between semantic and verbal uncertainty is a better predictor of hallucinations than semantic uncertainty alone.
Inference-time intervention on VUF (MUC) calibrates verbal uncertainty with semantic uncertainty, reducing confident hallucinations by an average of 29.6% in short-form QA tasks.
VUFs are consistent across different datasets and models, indicating a universal feature.
MUC improves the alignment between verbal and semantic uncertainty, as shown by increased correlation coefficients.
papers.limitation: The method may reduce correctness rate due to noise in semantic uncertainty measurement, leading to unnecessary abstentions.
papers.abstract: LLMs often adopt an assertive language style also when making false claims. Such ``overconfident hallucinations'' mislead users and erode trust. Achieving the ability to express in language the actual degree of uncertainty around a claim is therefore of great importance. We find that ``verbal uncertainty'' is governed by a single linear feature in the representation space of LLMs, and show that this has only moderate correlation with the actual ``semantic uncertainty'' of the model. We apply this insight and show that (1) the mismatch between semantic and verbal uncertainty is a better predictor of hallucinations than semantic uncertainty alone and (2) we can intervene on verbal uncertainty at inference time and reduce confident hallucinations on short-form answers, achieving an average relative reduction of ~30%.

papers.title: Inspecting and Editing Knowledge Representations in Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we map natural language statements to fact encodings in an LM's internal representations to enable editing and probing of knowledge?
papers.core_contribution: REMEDI is a method that learns to map natural language statements to fact encodings in LM representations, enabling both editing of knowledge (by adding vectors to hidden representations) and probing of existing knowledge.
papers.conclusion: REMEDI links work on probing, prompting, and LM editing, and offers steps toward general tools for fine-grained inspection and control of knowledge in LMs.
papers.key_findings:
REMEDI can patch errors made by an LM and insert new facts with or without context provided in the prompt.
REMEDI can help detect errors before generation by comparing edit vectors to unedited representations.
REMEDI increases accuracy on occupation classification and factual editing tasks compared to prompting baselines.
REMEDI generalizes from out-of-context training to in-context editing, suggesting unified representation of background and contextual knowledge.
REMEDI edits preserve correlations between features (e.g., adding 'made of metal' increases probability of 'shiny').
papers.limitation:
REMEDI can occasionally lead to disfluent or incorrect generations.
REMEDI sometimes damages the essence of the entity (e.g., making Wiener schnitzel an anime instead of a food).
REMEDI can also cause unrelated facts to change (e.g., changing the air dates of a TV show).
future_direction: Developing controlled generation interfaces that allow direct steering of model behavior in representation space.
Building tools for monitoring and controlling language generation by directly specifying facts and situations in an LM's native encoding scheme.
papers.abstract: Neural language models (LMs) represent facts about the world described by text. Sometimes these facts derive from training data (in most LMs, a representation of the word "banana" encodes the fact that bananas are fruits). Sometimes facts derive from input text itself (a representation of the sentence "I poured out the bottle" encodes the fact that the bottle became empty). We describe REMEDI, a method for learning to map statements in natural language to fact encodings in an LM's internal representation system. REMEDI encodings can be used as knowledge editors: when added to LM hidden representations, they modify downstream generation to be consistent with new facts. REMEDI encodings may also be used as probes: when compared to LM representations, they reveal which properties LMs already attribute to mentioned entities, in some cases making it possible to predict when LMs will generate outputs that conflict with background knowledge or input text. REMEDI thus links work on probing, prompting, and LM editing, and offers steps toward general tools for fine-grained inspection and control of knowledge in LMs.

papers.title: Confidence is Not Competence
papers.research_question: Why do large language models exhibit a disconnect between their internal confidence and actual problem-solving competence?
papers.core_contribution: The confidence-competence gap in LLMs is mechanistically explained by a decoupled two-system architecture: a high-dimensional assessment manifold for belief and a low-dimensional execution manifold for competence, with a sharp transition between them.
papers.conclusion: The confidence-competence gap is due to a decoupled two-system architecture, suggesting future work should focus on controlling the low-dimensional dynamics of execution rather than high-level assessment states.
papers.key_findings:
A linear probe can decode the model's 'solvability belief' from internal states, revealing a geometrically coherent belief axis.
Causal interventions that steer the belief state do not affect task performance, indicating the belief is causally inert.
The assessment manifold has high linear effective dimensionality, while the execution manifold is low-dimensional.
There is a sharp cognitive collapse from the assessment to execution phase, indicating a sequential two-system architecture.
This reveals an 'Assessment Brain' and an 'Execution Brain' that are geometrically and functionally distinct.
papers.limitation:
The findings are limited to tasks with unambiguous ground-truth solutions (e.g., math, logic, coding) and may not generalize to open-ended creative tasks.
The scaling laws of the cognitive collapse phenomenon are unknown and may vary with model size.
future_direction: Generalizing the 'Two Brains' model to open-ended creative tasks.
Studying the scaling laws of the cognitive collapse in larger models.
Developing 'mechanistic audits' to test Assessment and Execution brains separately.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) often exhibit a puzzling disconnect between their asserted confidence and actual problem-solving competence. We offer a mechanistic account of this decoupling by analyzing the geometry of internal states across two phases - pre-generative assessment and solution execution. A simple linear probe decodes the internal "solvability belief" of a model, revealing a well-ordered belief axis that generalizes across model families and across math, code, planning, and logic tasks. Yet, the geometries diverge - although belief is linearly decodable, the assessment manifold has high linear effective dimensionality as measured from the principal components, while the subsequent reasoning trace evolves on a much lower-dimensional manifold. This sharp reduction in geometric complexity from thought to action mechanistically explains the confidence-competence gap. Causal interventions that steer representations along the belief axis leave final solutions unchanged, indicating that linear nudges in the complex assessment space do not control the constrained dynamics of execution. We thus uncover a two-system architecture - a geometrically complex assessor feeding a geometrically simple executor. These results challenge the assumption that decodable beliefs are actionable levers, instead arguing for interventions that target the procedural dynamics of execution rather than the high-level geometry of assessment.

papers.title: On the Universal Truthfulness Hyperplane Inside LLMs
papers.research_question: Does a universal truthfulness hyperplane exist within LLMs that can distinguish factually correct and incorrect outputs?
papers.core_contribution: Increasing the diversity of training datasets significantly enhances the generalization of truthfulness probes, supporting the hypothesis that a universal truthfulness hyperplane exists within LLMs.
papers.conclusion: The findings support the existence of a universal truthfulness hyperplane in LLMs, offering directions for future research on hallucination mitigation.
papers.key_findings:
Probes trained on diverse datasets achieve ~70% cross-task accuracy, outperforming baselines like Self-Eval and Probability.
Attention head outputs are more effective for probing truthfulness than layer residual activations.
Increasing dataset diversity improves generalization more than increasing sample size.
The universal truthfulness hyperplane is more pronounced in advanced models like Mistral-7b and LLaMA2-13b-chat.
Probes trained on single datasets like TruthfulQA fail to generalize out-of-distribution, indicating overfitting.
papers.abstract: While large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable abilities across various fields, hallucination remains a significant challenge. Recent studies have explored hallucinations through the lens of internal representations, proposing mechanisms to decipher LLMs' adherence to facts. However, these approaches often fail to generalize to out-of-distribution data, leading to concerns about whether internal representation patterns reflect fundamental factual awareness, or only overfit spurious correlations on the specific datasets. In this work, we investigate whether a universal truthfulness hyperplane that distinguishes the model's factually correct and incorrect outputs exists within the model. To this end, we scale up the number of training datasets and conduct an extensive evaluation -- we train the truthfulness hyperplane on a diverse collection of over 40 datasets and examine its cross-task, cross-domain, and in-domain generalization. Our results indicate that increasing the diversity of the training datasets significantly enhances the performance in all scenarios, while the volume of data samples plays a less critical role. This finding supports the optimistic hypothesis that a universal truthfulness hyperplane may indeed exist within the model, offering promising directions for future research.

papers.title: Vision-Language Introspection: Mitigating Overconfident Hallucinations in MLLMs via Interpretable Bi-Causal Steering
papers.research_question: How to mitigate overconfident hallucinations in Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) by simulating a metacognitive self-correction process that diagnoses and rectifies internal visual-semantic misalignments?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Vision-Language Introspection (VLI), a training-free inference framework that mitigates object hallucinations in MLLMs by first introspectively localizing causal visual anchors and then performing interpretable bi-causal steering to rectify internal representations and calibrate overconfidence.
papers.conclusion: VLI effectively mitigates overconfident hallucinations in MLLMs by introspectively diagnosing visual-semantic conflicts and actively steering internal representations towards verified visual evidence, achieving state-of-the-art performance on standard benchmarks.
papers.key_findings:
VLI reduces the object hallucination rate by 12.67% on MMHal-Bench and improves accuracy by up to 6.33% on POPE compared to baseline models.
Bi-causal steering, which isolates visual evidence from background noise via counterfactual representations, is the most critical component for error rectification.
The method successfully localizes interpretable visual anchors corresponding to high-risk tokens, enabling precise intervention.
VLI demonstrates robust generalization across diverse datasets (MSCOCO, A-OKVQA, GQA) and model architectures (LLaVA-1.5, Qwen3-VL).
Adaptive confidence calibration effectively penalizes ungrounded certainty, mitigating persistent hallucinations driven by blind confidence.
papers.limitation: The method introduces increased computational latency and memory overhead due to the parallel processing of counterfactual branches, though optimization reduces the impact.
papers.abstract: Object hallucination critically undermines the reliability of Multimodal Large Language Models, often stemming from a fundamental failure in cognitive introspection, where models blindly trust linguistic priors over specific visual evidence. Existing mitigations remain limited: contrastive decoding approaches operate superficially without rectifying internal semantic misalignments, while current latent steering methods rely on static vectors that lack instance-specific precision. We introduce Vision-Language Introspection (VLI), a training-free inference framework that simulates a metacognitive self-correction process. VLI first performs Attributive Introspection to diagnose hallucination risks via probabilistic conflict detection and localize the causal visual anchors. It then employs Interpretable Bi-Causal Steering to actively modulate the inference process, dynamically isolating visual evidence from background noise while neutralizing blind confidence through adaptive calibration. VLI achieves state-of-the-art performance on advanced models, reducing object hallucination rates by 12.67% on MMHal-Bench and improving accuracy by 5.8% on POPE.

papers.title: Intrinsic Self-correction for Enhanced Morality: An Analysis of Internal Mechanisms and the Superficial Hypothesis
papers.research_question: The paper investigates three research questions: (1) In what scenarios does moral self-correction work? (2) What are the internal mechanisms of LLMs influenced by self-correction instructions? (3) Is intrinsic moral self-correction actually superficial?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes that intrinsic moral self-correction in LLMs is superficial, as it only provides a shortcut to moral outputs without significantly reducing immorality in internal hidden states.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that intrinsic moral self-correction is superficial, relying on shortcuts rather than fundamentally reducing immorality in LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
Self-correction works best when the correct answer is already top-ranked.
Morality levels in intermediate hidden states are strong indicators of instruction effectiveness.
Self-correction reduces immorality in attention heads but increases it in feed-forward layers for QA tasks.
The slight difference in hidden states with and without self-correction supports the superficial hypothesis.
Internal hidden states can be used to predict the effectiveness of self-correction instructions.
papers.limitation:
The exact underlying reason for the superficial phenomenon is not uncovered.
Defining superficial self-correction is challenging.
future_direction: Automating methods for optimizing instruction development for self-correction.
Exploring fine-tuning to enhance LLMs' self-correction capabilities.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are capable of producing content that perpetuates stereotypes, discrimination, and toxicity. The recently proposed moral self-correction is a computationally efficient method for reducing harmful content in the responses of LLMs. However, the process of how injecting self-correction instructions can modify the behavior of LLMs remains under-explored. In this paper, we explore the effectiveness of moral self-correction by answering three research questions: (1) In what scenarios does moral self-correction work? (2) What are the internal mechanisms of LLMs, e.g., hidden states, that are influenced by moral self-correction instructions? (3) Is intrinsic moral self-correction actually superficial in terms of reduced immorality in hidden states? We argue that self-correction can help LLMs find a shortcut to more morally correct output, rather than truly reducing the immorality stored in hidden states. Through empirical investigation with tasks of language generation and multi-choice question answering, we conclude:(i) LLMs exhibit good performance across both tasks, and self-correction instructions are particularly beneficial when the correct answer is already top-ranked; (ii) The morality levels in intermediate hidden states are strong indicators as to whether one instruction would be more effective than another; (iii) Based on our analysis of intermediate hidden states and task case studies of self-correction behaviors, we are first to propose the hypothesis that intrinsic moral self-correction is in fact superficial.

papers.title: Mind Scramble: Unveiling Large Language Model Psychology Via Typoglycemia
papers.research_question: Does LLM possess human-like cognitive processes and mechanisms in reading and comprehending? The paper uses Typoglycemia to explore this.
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces LLM Psychology, a framework that uses Typoglycemia experiments to study cognitive behaviors of LLMs. It finds that LLMs exhibit human-like behaviors but are fundamentally data-driven, and each LLM has a unique cognitive pattern.
papers.conclusion: The study advances research on aligning LLMs with human cognition and provides evidence that LLMs' abilities are data-driven, offering a case for LLM Psychology.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs demonstrate human-like behaviors on a macro scale, such as slightly lower task accuracy with consuming more tokens and time.
Different LLMs show varying degrees of robustness to scrambled input, making it a democratized benchmark for model evaluation.
The impact of different task types varies, with complex logical tasks (e.g., math) in scrambled format being more challenging.
LLMs' emergent human-like abilities are fundamentally statistical and data-driven, rather than genuinely resembling human cognition.
Each LLM exhibits its unique and consistent 'cognitive pattern' across various tasks, unveiling a general mechanism in its psychology process.
papers.abstract: Research into the external behaviors and internal mechanisms of large language models (LLMs) has shown promise in addressing complex tasks in the physical world. Studies suggest that powerful LLMs, like GPT-4, are beginning to exhibit human-like cognitive abilities, including planning, reasoning, and reflection. In this paper, we introduce a research line and methodology called LLM Psychology, leveraging human psychology experiments to investigate the cognitive behaviors and mechanisms of LLMs. We migrate the Typoglycemia phenomenon from psychology to explore the "mind" of LLMs. Unlike human brains, which rely on context and word patterns to comprehend scrambled text, LLMs use distinct encoding and decoding processes. Through Typoglycemia experiments at the character, word, and sentence levels, we observe: (I) LLMs demonstrate human-like behaviors on a macro scale, such as lower task accuracy and higher token/time consumption; (II) LLMs exhibit varying robustness to scrambled input, making Typoglycemia a benchmark for model evaluation without new datasets; (III) Different task types have varying impacts, with complex logical tasks (e.g., math) being more challenging in scrambled form; (IV) Each LLM has a unique and consistent "cognitive pattern" across tasks, revealing general mechanisms in its psychology process. We provide an in-depth analysis of hidden layers to explain these phenomena, paving the way for future research in LLM Psychology and deeper interpretability.

papers.title: ShortGPT: Layers in Large Language Models are More Redundant Than You Expect
papers.research_question: How redundant are the layers in large language models, and can a simple layer removal method based on a new importance metric effectively prune them?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies significant layer redundancy in LLMs and introduces Block Influence (BI) to measure layer importance. Based on BI, the proposed ShortGPT method removes redundant layers, achieving competitive pruning results without fine-tuning.
papers.conclusion: LLMs exhibit significant layer-wise redundancy, and a simple pruning method based on layer removal (ShortGPT) can effectively compress models with minimal performance loss, offering insights for future model compression and training efficiency.
papers.key_findings:
Layers in LLMs are redundant, especially in the middle to later layers, and removing them individually causes minimal performance degradation.
The proposed Block Influence (BI) metric, based on cosine similarity between a layer's input and output hidden states, correlates with layer importance.
ShortGPT, a simple layer removal method based on BI, outperforms previous state-of-the-art pruning methods and maintains ~90% performance while reducing ~25% parameters.
The redundancy phenomenon is not unique to transformers; it also exists in non-transformer models like Mamba and RWKV.
ShortGPT is orthogonal to quantization and can be combined with it for further compression.
papers.limitation: Layer removal has a more significant negative effect on generative tasks compared to multiple-choice tasks, especially for smaller models.
future_direction: Exploring post-training to restore performance after pruning
Improving model training efficiency by reducing inherent redundancy
papers.abstract: As Large Language Models (LLMs) continue to advance in performance, their size has escalated significantly, with current LLMs containing billions or even trillions of parameters. However, in this study, we discovered that many layers of LLMs exhibit high similarity, and some layers play a negligible role in network functionality. Based on this observation, we define a metric called Block Influence (BI) to gauge the significance of each layer in LLMs. We then propose a straightforward pruning approach: layer removal, in which we directly delete the redundant layers in LLMs based on their BI scores. Experiments demonstrate that our method, which we call ShortGPT, significantly outperforms previous state-of-the-art (SOTA) methods in model pruning. Moreover, ShortGPT is orthogonal to quantization-like methods, enabling further reduction in parameters and computation. The ability to achieve better results through simple layer removal, as opposed to more complex pruning techniques, suggests a high degree of redundancy in the model architecture.

papers.title: TruthX: Alleviating Hallucinations by Editing Large Language Models in Truthful Space
papers.research_question: How to alleviate hallucinations in Large Language Models by editing their internal representations in a truthful space?
papers.core_contribution: TruthX is an inference-time intervention method that enhances the truthfulness of LLMs by mapping their internal representations to truthful and semantic latent spaces, identifying a truthful editing direction, and editing the representations in the truthful space.
papers.conclusion: TruthX effectively enhances the truthfulness of LLMs by editing their internal representations in a truthful space, demonstrating significant improvements across multiple benchmarks and models.
papers.key_findings:
TruthX improves the truthfulness of 13 advanced LLMs by an average of 20% on the TruthfulQA benchmark.
TruthX can control an LLM to produce truthful or hallucinatory responses by editing only one vector in the LLM's internal representations.
The truthful space extracted from homologous LLMs (trained sequentially) exhibits high similarity, allowing a well-trained TruthX to be directly applied to different homologous models.
Layer-wise analysis indicates that representations in the middle layers of LLMs have a higher correlation with the truthfulness of responses.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) sometimes suffer from producing hallucinations, especially LLMs may generate untruthful responses despite knowing the correct knowledge. Activating the truthfulness within LLM is the key to fully unlocking LLM's knowledge potential. In this paper, we propose TruthX, an inference-time intervention method to activate the truthfulness of LLM by identifying and editing the features within LLM's internal representations that govern the truthfulness. TruthX employs an auto-encoder to map LLM's representations into semantic and truthful latent spaces respectively, and applies contrastive learning to identify a truthful editing direction within the truthful space. During inference, by editing LLM's internal representations in truthful space, TruthX effectively enhances the truthfulness of LLM. Experiments show that TruthX improves the truthfulness of 13 advanced LLMs by an average of 20% on TruthfulQA benchmark. Further analyses suggest that TruthX can control LLM to produce truthful or hallucinatory responses via editing only one vector in LLM's internal representations.

papers.title: NeST: Neuron Selective Tuning for LLM Safety
papers.research_question: How can we achieve efficient and effective safety alignment in large language models by selectively tuning safety-relevant neurons?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces NeST, a lightweight, structure-aware safety alignment framework that selectively adapts safety-relevant neurons by clustering them and applying shared updates, achieving strong safety performance with extreme parameter efficiency.
papers.conclusion: NeST provides a practical, efficient, and effective method for safety alignment in LLMs, enabling targeted adaptation of safety behavior with minimal parameter updates.
papers.key_findings:
NeST reduces the average attack success rate from 44.5% to 4.36%, a 90.2% reduction in unsafe generations.
NeST requires only 0.44 million trainable parameters on average, a 17,310× decrease compared to full fine-tuning and 9.25× reduction relative to LoRA.
NeST consistently achieves stronger safety performance than LoRA and Circuit Breaker across 10 open-weight LLMs.
NeST preserves core model capabilities on standard reasoning and knowledge benchmarks.
NeST remains robust across diverse inference settings and input modalities, including text-only and multimodal generation.
papers.limitation: NeST relies on a safety-aligned base model and a diverse set of prompts for safety neuron detection, which may not be available in all settings.
future_direction: Extending NeST to other model families and architectures.
Automating the selection of hyperparameters such as the number of clusters.
Applying NeST to other tasks beyond safety, such as task-specific adaptation.
papers.abstract: Safety alignment is essential for the responsible deployment of large language models (LLMs). Yet, existing approaches often rely on heavyweight fine-tuning that is costly to update, audit, and maintain across model families. Full fine-tuning incurs substantial computational and storage overhead, while parameter-efficient methods such as LoRA trade efficiency for inconsistent safety gains and sensitivity to design choices. Safety intervention mechanisms such as circuit breakers reduce unsafe outputs without modifying model weights, but do not directly shape or preserve the internal representations that govern safety behavior. These limitations hinder rapid and reliable safety updates, particularly in settings where models evolve frequently or must adapt to new policies and domains. We present NeST, a lightweight, structure-aware safety alignment framework that strengthens refusal behavior by selectively adapting a small subset of safety-relevant neurons while freezing the remainder of the model. NeST aligns parameter updates with the internal organization of safety behavior by clustering functionally coherent safety neurons and enforcing shared updates within each cluster, enabling targeted and stable safety adaptation without broad model modification or inference-time overhead. We benchmark NeST against three dominant baselines: full fine-tuning, LoRA-based fine-tuning, and circuit breakers across 10 open-weight LLMs spanning multiple model families and sizes. Across all evaluated models, NeST reduces the attack success rate from an average of 44.5% to 4.36%, corresponding to a 90.2% reduction in unsafe generations, while requiring only 0.44 million trainable parameters on average. This amounts to a 17,310x decrease in updated parameters compared to full fine-tuning and a 9.25x reduction relative to LoRA, while consistently achieving stronger safety performance for alignment.

papers.title: Energy-Driven Steering: Reducing False Refusals in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we reduce false refusals (over-refusal) in aligned large language models without compromising safety, using a fine-tuning free, inference-time intervention?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Energy Landscape Steering (ELS), a fine-tuning free framework that uses an externally trained Energy-Based Model to dynamically steer LLM hidden activations during inference, significantly reducing false refusals while maintaining safety and general capabilities.
papers.conclusion: ELS establishes a promising paradigm for building LLMs that simultaneously achieve high safety and low false refusal rates through inference-time activation steering.
papers.key_findings:
ELS raises compliance on the ORB-H false refusal benchmark from 57.3% to 82.6% for Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct while maintaining baseline safety performance.
ELS outperforms existing fine-tuning free methods (Surgical, CAST, AdaSteer, AlphaSteer) in reducing false refusals without degrading safety or general knowledge.
ELS preserves general capabilities (MMLU, ARC-C, MATH accuracy) almost entirely, unlike fine-tuning methods which often degrade them.
ELS shows robustness against multi-turn jailbreak attacks, maintaining lower attack success rates compared to baselines.
The method is computationally efficient, adding minimal overhead during inference compared to other steering techniques.
papers.limitation:
ELS relies on an EBM trained on a fixed dataset, limiting its adaptability to emerging jailbreak tactics unseen during training.
Data labeling operates at the response level, not capturing partial compliance or mid-response refusal patterns, which could be beneficial for reasoning models.
future_direction: Make ELS an online method where the EBM continuously updates based on new interaction data.
Extend data labeling to a more fine-grained, sentence-level annotation scheme to capture partial compliance patterns.
Apply the method to reasoning models with chain-of-thought to rescue misaligned refusals during the thinking period.
papers.abstract: Safety alignment of large language models (LLMs) faces a key challenge: current alignment techniques often only focus on improving safety against harmful prompts, causing LLMs to become over-cautious and refuse to respond to benign prompts. Therefore, a key objective of safe alignment is to enhance safety while simultaneously reducing false refusals. In this paper, we introduce Energy-Driven Steering (EDS), a novel, fine-tuning free framework designed to resolve this challenge through dynamic, inference-time intervention. We trained a lightweight, external Energy-Based Model (EBM) to assign high energy to undesirable (false refusal or jailbreak) states and low energy to desirable (helpful response or safe reject) ones. During inference, EBM maps the LLM's internal activations to an "energy landscape". We use the gradient of the energy function to dynamically steer the LLM's hidden states to low energy regions, correcting the model to generate a desirable response in real-time without modifying its weights. This method decouples behavioral control from the model's core knowledge, offering a flexible solution with minimal computational overhead. Extensive experiments across a wide range of models show our method successfully achieves this objective: it substantially lowers false refusal rates. For example, raising compliance on the ORB-H benchmark from 57.3% to 82.6% while maintaining the baseline safety performance. Our work presents an effective paradigm for building LLMs that achieve both low false refusal rates and high safety.

papers.title: Distilled Circuits: A Mechanistic Study of Internal Restructuring in Knowledge Distillation
papers.research_question: How does knowledge distillation restructure internal circuits and representations in student models, and how can functional alignment between teacher and student be quantified?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides a mechanistic understanding of how knowledge distillation restructures internal circuits, showing that students compress and discard teacher components, and introduces an alignment metric to quantify functional alignment beyond output similarity.
papers.conclusion: While student models preserve broad functional behavior from their teachers, knowledge distillation causes significant internal circuit restructuring, leading to increased reliance on fewer components and reduced robustness. The alignment metric captures functional similarity beyond output behavior.
papers.key_findings:
Student models reorganize, compress, and discard teacher components, leading to stronger reliance on fewer components.
Student models are more vulnerable to component ablation, indicating reduced robustness.
The introduced alignment metric effectively quantifies functional alignment between teacher and student models.
These findings on internal restructuring and reduced robustness generalize across different model architectures (GPT2, BERT, Llama).
Performance similarity does not guarantee similarity in internal computation; circuit-level analysis is essential for understanding functional alignment.
papers.limitation:
The study is constrained by the relatively small set of models evaluated (6).
The component role attribution procedure is manual and could be automated.
The alignment metric could be improved in granularity and interpretability.
The findings are based on specific tasks and models and may not generalize to all settings.
future_direction: Apply the methodology and alignment metric to a broader, more diverse collection of models.
Automate the component role attribution procedure, potentially using interpretability agents.
Improve the alignment metric's granularity and interpretability, and explore incorporating it as a loss term during distillation.
papers.abstract: Knowledge distillation compresses a larger neural model (teacher) into smaller, faster student models by training them to match teacher outputs. However, the internal computational transformations that occur during this process remain poorly understood. We apply techniques from mechanistic interpretability to analyze how internal circuits, representations, and activation patterns differ between teacher and student. Focusing on GPT2-small and its distilled counterpart DistilGPT2, we find that student models reorganize, compress, and discard teacher components, often resulting in stronger reliance on fewer individual components. To quantify functional alignment beyond output similarity, we introduce an alignment metric based on influence-weighted component similarity, validated across multiple tasks. Our findings reveal that while knowledge distillation preserves broad functional behaviors, it also causes significant shifts in internal computation, with important implications for the robustness and generalization capacity of distilled models.

papers.title: How Alignment and Jailbreak Work: Explain LLM Safety through Intermediate Hidden States
papers.research_question: How do alignment and jailbreak work in large language models? The paper investigates the mechanisms of safety alignment and how jailbreak circumvents it by analyzing intermediate hidden states.
papers.core_contribution: LLMs learn ethical concepts during pre-training and can identify malicious inputs in early layers. Safety alignment associates these early concepts with positive/negative emotions in middle layers, which are refined into accept/reject tokens. Jailbreak works by disturbing this association.
papers.conclusion: The work explains how alignment and jailbreak function through intermediate hidden states, enhancing transparency and offering a new perspective for LLM safety development.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs learn ethical concepts during pre-training, not just from alignment.
Weak classifiers can distinguish malicious and normal inputs from early layer hidden states with >95% accuracy.
Alignment associates early ethical concepts with emotion guesses (positive/negative) in middle layers, which are refined into stylistic accept/reject tokens.
Jailbreak does not deceive early ethical classification but disturbs the association between early and middle layers.
Logit Grafting, which grafts positive emotions onto malicious inputs, approximates jailbreak and confirms the disturbance mechanism.
papers.limitation: Used default settings of simple weak classifiers and only examined safety perspective; method might generalize to other capabilities but not tested.
future_direction: Apply the method to interpret other capabilities of LLMs.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) rely on safety alignment to avoid responding to malicious user inputs. Unfortunately, jailbreak can circumvent safety guardrails, resulting in LLMs generating harmful content and raising concerns about LLM safety. Due to language models with intensive parameters often regarded as black boxes, the mechanisms of alignment and jailbreak are challenging to elucidate. In this paper, we employ weak classifiers to explain LLM safety through the intermediate hidden states. We first confirm that LLMs learn ethical concepts during pre-training rather than alignment and can identify malicious and normal inputs in the early layers. Alignment actually associates the early concepts with emotion guesses in the middle layers and then refines them to the specific reject tokens for safe generations.
